transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, honestly, I didn't really even think I needed to come in, but the people at the regular clinic just kept getting on me. They were getting all worked up and on my case about how little I've been eating lately. But I mean, you have to understand my schedule, it's just really packed right now and I have a lot going on. Most days I'm up super early, and I'm just grabbing a coffee before I head to the warehouse. I work as a packer, so I'm on my feet all day, boxing things up, taping, moving around constantly, and you really don't have time to just sit around and eat anyway. It slows you down, you know? 

And then after my shift, I have my GED classes. I've been really trying to finish that up since I never got my diploma back in high school, so my brain is just going in a million different directions all day. By the time class is over, maybe I'll have a yogurt or just, I don't know, a few bites of something small. It's just... if I actually stop and sit down for a real, full meal, it feels like it throws off everything. Like, my whole routine, my focus, everything I’m trying to keep in line just gets completely messed up and heavy. So I just keep it light and keep moving, but the clinic made it sound like this huge emergency, which I just don't really see, because I'm getting everything done that I need to, but... well, anyway, that's why they told me I had to come see you.
Do you ever think about your weight when deciding how much to eat?

Well, I mean... yeah, I guess I do. I think most people probably do, right? But for me, it's just... it's kind of always there in the back of my head. Like, at the warehouse, for example, people are always bringing junk into the break room. Someone's always ordering fried food, or bringing in donuts for a birthday or whatever, and it's just sitting there. And if I even think about having some of that fried food, or, oh, like on Sundays when I go to church and they have those big potlucks afterwards... if I were to actually sit down with a big plate of food there, I just... I get so scared. 

I get this horrible, panicky feeling that if I eat it, it’s going to show on me right away. Like, literally right away, like people will be able to look at me and just see it instantly attached to my body. And if I do happen to eat something like that, I just can't let it go. I'll keep thinking about it the entire rest of my shift, just turning it over and over in my head while I'm taping up boxes, stressing about what it's doing to my body. It just plays on a loop. It honestly drives me crazy until I can finally get home and check the scale. I just get this overwhelming urge where I have to check the scale to see the damage, just to make sure it didn't instantly change me or make me bigger. 

So, yeah, I guess my weight is pretty much the main thing I'm thinking about when I look at food, because the anxiety of it showing on me is just way too much to deal with. It's just easier to stick to my routine and not touch it.
Do you ever make yourself vomit after eating?

No, no, I don't do that. I know some people do, like you hear about it on TV or whatever, but I've never actually made myself throw up. The thought of it just kind of grosses me out, honestly. Plus, with my schedule, I don't even know when I would have the time or the privacy to do something like that. At the warehouse, the bathrooms are always busy, there's always someone coming in or out, especially during break times when everyone rushes in there at once. And then at GED classes, it's the same thing, just a tiny little restroom down the hall that echoes, so everyone can hear everything. 

And besides, like I said, I barely eat enough to even need to do something like that anyway. If I'm just having my coffee in the morning and maybe a yogurt at night, there's really nothing to get rid of, you know? It just seems like so much extra work and mess when I can just control what goes in to begin with. It's so much cleaner and easier to just not eat the bad stuff in the first place. Like, why put myself through the stress of eating a donut and then the stress of trying to throw it up, when I can just walk past the break room table and avoid the whole situation entirely? It just makes more sense to me to keep my routine tight and not even open that door. So, no, throwing up is definitely not something I do. I just rely on my willpower to keep things in check.
Do you exercise to try to control your weight?

Well, I mean, not really in the traditional sense, I guess. Like, I don't have a gym membership or anything like that. I don't go running on a treadmill for hours or take spin classes or whatever people do. Honestly, who has the money or the time for that? By the time I get off my shift at the warehouse, I am just exhausted. I mean, my job is basically a workout in itself. I'm lifting boxes, taping them, stacking them on pallets, walking back and forth across this massive concrete floor all day long. My pedometer app on my phone says I hit, like, 15,000 to 20,000 steps a day just at work alone. 

So, it's not like I'm doing jumping jacks in my living room to burn off calories, because I'm already moving so much. And then I have to hustle to catch the bus to get to my GED classes, and sometimes if the bus is running late, which it almost always is on Tuesdays and Thursdays for some reason, I end up having to speed-walk or even jog the last six blocks from the transit center to the adult ed building just so I'm not walking in late and having the instructor give me that look, you know? 

So between all of that, I feel like I'm constantly burning energy anyway. I don't really need to set aside specific time to exercise just to control my weight, because my whole life is just one big cycle of moving and working and trying to get things done. If anything, I rely on the fact that I'm always on my feet to keep things balanced. But as far as, like, putting on workout clothes and doing a routine? No, I don't do that. I just let my schedule do the work for me, if that makes sense.
Do you think your weight is actually lower than what other people might think it is?

Well, um... I guess I think people are just kind of overreacting, honestly. Like, I know my regular doctor mentioned something about my weight being low at my last physical, and... and some of the ladies at church, they've been giving me these looks lately, or trying to push extra food on me during the potlucks, whispering to each other like I can't hear them. It's so frustrating because they act like I'm wasting away or something, but I honestly don't see what the big deal is. I mean, they look at me and they seem to think I'm in some kind of danger, but I really think they're making it into a much bigger deal than it actually is. 

If my weight was really that dangerously low, or if I was as sick as they seem to think I am, how could I still be doing everything I'm doing? I'm still getting up every single morning, taking the bus in the dark, and working an eight-hour shift at the warehouse, lifting heavy boxes and walking miles on concrete. And then I still go to my GED classes two nights a week. I'm keeping up with my life, you know? I'm paying my rent, I'm doing my laundry, I'm managing everything on my own. It's not like I'm bedridden or passing out at work. So when people get all worried and act like my weight is this huge crisis, I just feel like they're totally exaggerating. I look in the mirror and I just see... me. I see someone who is functioning perfectly fine. So, no, I don't think my weight is lower than what they think... I think they just don't understand that I'm actually doing okay.
Do you think you would be happy with your weight if other people stopped commenting on it?

Well, I mean, it would be nice if people stopped commenting, sure. It gets really old, really fast, especially at church or when I'm just trying to get through my shift at the warehouse without someone asking if I ate breakfast. But... no, I don't think I'd be completely happy with it, honestly. It's not just about what they think or what they say. It's about what I see, you know? 

Like, when I'm getting ready in the morning, or right before I head out to my GED classes, I'll look in the mirror, and... I just don't see what they see. I look at my stomach, or I look at my thighs, and they just... they still look bigger than they should. It's like, no matter what the scale says or what the ladies at church are whispering about, my eyes are telling me something different. I can see the areas that still need work. And it's so frustrating because it really dictates my whole mood. 

If I wake up and I look in the mirror and things feel a little tighter, a little more controlled, then I feel like, okay, I'm doing good today. I'm on track. I can go to work, I can handle the boxes, I can focus in class. But if I look in the mirror and my stomach looks puffy, or my thighs are touching in a way I don't like, it just ruins everything. It feels like I'm failing. And that feeling just hangs over me for the entire day. I'll be standing there taping a box at work, and all I can think about is how I failed, how I need to do better, how I can't let myself slip. So, even if everyone else in the world just shut up about my weight, I'd still have to deal with that mirror. I'd still have to deal with how my stomach and my thighs look to me, and how that one glance in the morning basically decides if I'm succeeding or failing for the next twenty-four hours. So, no, their comments stopping wouldn't fix the real issue, which is just... how I look to myself.
Do you think your body shape or weight is different from how others see it?

Yeah, I mean, that really just goes back to what I was just trying to explain about the mirror. There is definitely a huge disconnect between what they see and what I see. Because, like, they're all acting like I'm wasting away, right? But when I look in the mirror—whether it's right before I head out to my GED class, or even before I go play softball... I play in this weekend rec league sometimes, just to get out of the house and do something normal, you know? Anyway, when I look in the mirror before class or softball, my stomach and my thighs still look bigger than they should. 

I'll stand there in my bathroom, under that awful, harsh fluorescent light we have, and I can just see it. I can see where my thighs are touching, or where my stomach isn't perfectly flat, and it's like... how can other people not see this? How can the ladies at church look at me and think I'm too thin when I can literally see the areas that still need so much work? It's crazy to me. I honestly think they're just not looking closely, or maybe they just have really skewed standards, I don't know. 

And it really does just take over my whole brain. Like I was saying, it can completely make me feel like I’m either doing good or failing for the whole day. If I put on my softball pants and they feel even a tiny bit snug on my thighs, or if I catch a glimpse of my stomach looking puffy in the mirror before class, I just feel like a massive failure. It just crashes down on me. I'll be out there in the outfield waiting for a fly ball, or sitting at my desk trying to focus on algebra equations, and all I can think about is how I messed up, how my body is wrong, and how I need to fix it. I can't even enjoy the game or focus on the teacher because I'm just so hyper-aware of how big my thighs feel in my pants. But on the flip side, if I look in the mirror and things look smaller, or my stomach is perfectly flat, then I feel like I'm succeeding. I feel light, I feel focused, I feel like I can take on the world. So, yes, what I see is completely, one hundred percent different from whatever it is they think they're looking at.
Do you think your body shape is normal?

I mean, normal is... well, like I was just saying a second ago, it really comes down to that mirror. I know I'm kind of repeating myself, but it's just because it's the absolute truth of my life right now, and it's hard to talk about anything else. So, no, I don't think my shape is "normal" yet, because it's not where it needs to be. 

Like I mentioned, when I look in the mirror before my GED class, or when I'm getting dressed for a softball game, my stomach and my thighs... they just still look so much bigger than they should. They just do. And I know I just told you how that makes me feel, but I don't know if I can even fully explain how much it dictates literally everything I do. It completely decides if I’m doing good or if I’m failing for the entire day. 

If I don't look right to myself—if there's still that extra puffiness on my stomach or if my thighs are too wide—then I am failing. I'll be at the warehouse, just trying to pack my quota of boxes, and I can feel my thighs touching when I walk down the concrete aisles, and it just ruins me. I feel heavy and wrong and totally abnormal. It's like this dark cloud just follows me around the warehouse floor. But if I look in that mirror in the morning and I see that things are smaller, tighter... then I feel like I'm succeeding. Then I feel what I imagine "normal" is supposed to feel like. I feel light and capable. So until my stomach and thighs actually look the way they're supposed to, instead of being too big, I can't say my shape is normal. It's just... it's a work in progress, I guess, and right now, that progress is just making me feel like I'm failing way more often than I'm succeeding.
Do you think you would look different to yourself if you were at a weight that others consider healthy?

If I was at a weight that *they* consider healthy? Oh, wow. I mean... I know I'm sounding like a broken record here, and I'm sorry if I'm just talking in circles, but it really just all comes back to exactly what I've been saying. If I weighed what the ladies at church or whoever think I should weigh, I can't even imagine how awful I would look to myself. 

Because right now, even at the weight I'm at, when I look in the mirror before class or before I go to play softball... my stomach and my thighs still look bigger than they should. They just do. So if I actually gained weight to be "healthy" by their standards? Those areas would look enormous to me. It would be an absolute nightmare. Because, like I've been trying to explain, what I see in that bathroom mirror isn't just a passing thought. It completely takes over. It can make me feel like I’m either doing good or failing for the whole day. 

If I were at their version of a healthy weight, I would just be failing. Every single day, without exception. I'd wake up, look at my thighs touching even more than they already do, look at my stomach sticking out, and I would just know I failed. I wouldn't be able to tape a single box at the warehouse without feeling completely disgusted with myself. I wouldn't be able to run bases at softball because I'd just feel so heavy and wrong in my uniform. 

So, yes, I would look different to myself, but in the absolute worst way possible. It wouldn't magically fix the way I see my body or make me happy. It would just make the things I already hate—the puffiness, the width of my legs—so much worse. I'd just be handing myself a failing grade before I even walked out the door for my GED classes. I just... I can't even entertain the idea of that, honestly, because just trying to manage how big those areas look to me right now is already taking up all my mental energy. I'm just trying to get to a point where I don't feel like a failure, and gaining weight would just guarantee that I feel like one permanently.
Do you think your body looks the way you think it does when you look in the mirror?

I know I literally keep saying the exact same thing over and over, and you're probably getting so tired of hearing about my bathroom mirror, but yes. Yes, I absolutely believe that my body looks exactly the way I see it. It’s not like I’m looking into a funhouse mirror, you know? It’s just a standard, cheap piece of glass from the hardware store. I'm not hallucinating. 

Like I’ve been trying to explain, whenever I look in that mirror before I leave for my GED class, or before I go to the park for softball, I am seeing the reality of my body. My stomach and my thighs still look bigger than they should. I can see the actual shape of them. I can see where they take up too much space. And I know I keep coming back to how that affects me, but it’s because it’s so completely overwhelming. Seeing those areas look so big... it can make me feel like I’m either doing good or failing for the whole entire day. 

If I see that extra width, I don't stand there and think, "Oh, my eyes must be playing tricks on me." I think, "I am failing." And it’s so real to me that I physically feel it for the rest of the day. If I see my stomach sticking out in that mirror, I will feel it pressing against the waistband of my jeans the entire shift while I'm packing boxes at the warehouse. It’s like a physical weight I have to drag around. I don't understand how other people can look at the exact same physical body and claim they don't see what I see. It honestly makes me feel like I'm losing my mind sometimes, trying to figure out how they are missing it. But then I go back home, I look in the mirror again, and there it is. The proof is right there. So, yeah, I believe what I see. I have to. It's right in front of my face.
Do you think your perception of your body shape is accurate?

I feel like... I mean, aren't you just asking me the same thing again? I really don't want to be difficult, I promise, but I feel like we're just going around in circles here and I don't know how else to explain it to you. Yes, I think my perception is accurate. I really, truly do. Because, like I've been saying this whole time, I'm not just imagining things out of nowhere. 

When I stand there and look in the mirror before my GED class, or when I'm getting my gear together for softball... I'm looking at my actual, physical body. And my stomach and my thighs still look bigger than they should. That is just the absolute truth. I can see it with my own two eyes. I can literally pinch the parts that are wrong. I can feel them rubbing together when I'm walking down the concrete aisles packing boxes at work. 

So if you're asking if my brain is somehow tricking me or making me see things that aren't there, no, I don't think so at all. My perception has to be accurate because of how real the consequences are. Like I keep telling you, seeing those areas look so big... it completely takes over my entire life. It literally makes me feel like I’m either doing good or failing for the whole day. If I see that my thighs are too wide in the morning, I carry that failure with me to the warehouse, to class, to the softball field... everywhere. It's a physical weight on my chest. If my perception wasn't accurate, why would I feel it so intensely? Why would it completely ruin my entire shift if it wasn't real? I just... I know what I look like. I know exactly what I see. And I know that it's accurate, which is why I'm so desperate to fix it.
Was there a particular event or experience that made you start worrying about gaining weight?

I don't know if there was just one single, big event from my past, like a lightbulb moment or some huge dramatic thing where I just woke up and started worrying. It's not really like that for me. It's more about... specific situations that happen, like everyday experiences that just set off this huge, uncontrollable panic in my head. 

Like, at work, in the warehouse break room. Sometimes people bring in food, or there's fried food in there, and everyone is just eating it so casually. Or at church, you know, after the service when they have those big get-togethers and everyone is just loading up these massive plates of food. If I try to participate... if I eat something like fried food from the break room or a big plate at church, it's just immediate panic. I get so incredibly scared that it’s going to show on me right away. Like, literally the second I swallow it, I feel like I can feel it expanding my stomach or going straight to my thighs. 

And once I eat it, I can't just move on with my day like a normal person. I’ll keep thinking about it, over and over, the entire rest of my shift. I'll be standing there taping up packages, and all I can think is, "You ate that, it's showing, you're bigger now." It just plays on a loop. It gets so loud and so overwhelming that all I want to do is check the scale. I just get this desperate need to go home and step on the scale to see the damage, to see if it made me heavier right that exact second. So it's not really one event from years ago that started it all... it's just that every single time I'm in a situation with food like that, it becomes this whole terrifying event all over again, and I just can't stop obsessing over the weight I might have just put on.
Was there a traumatic event in your past that you associate with gaining weight or being overweight?

I feel like... wait, didn't you just ask me almost this exact same thing? About an event? I'm not trying to be rude, I just... I feel like I'm repeating myself a lot today. 

Like a big, dramatic trauma? Like something out of a movie? No. I don't have some dark, repressed memory of someone calling me fat when I was seven, or some horrible tragedy that made me this way. I really don't. I know you're trying to find the root cause or some big psychological trigger or whatever, but like I literally just finished saying a second ago, the trauma for me is just... it's just everyday life. It's the food itself. 

Those situations I was just talking about? That *is* the traumatic event for me, every single time it happens. If I eat something like fried food from the break room at the warehouse, or if I'm at church and I have a big plate of food at the fellowship dinner... it's just pure, immediate panic. I get so incredibly scared that it’s going to show on me right away. Like, instantly. I'll take a bite of whatever someone brought into the break room—say it's some greasy fried chicken or whatever—and the second I swallow it, my heart starts racing. I'm terrified that it's just immediately attaching itself to my thighs or pushing my stomach out against my jeans. 

And I can't just brush it off like a normal person would. I will keep thinking about it. I'll go back out to the warehouse floor, I'll be packing boxes, pulling the tape gun, stacking things on the pallets, and my brain is just screaming at me. "You ate that, it's showing, everyone can see it, you're bigger." It's this huge, overwhelming panic that just loops and loops and loops for the rest of my shift. And the only thing I can think about, the absolute *only* thing that will make that screaming in my head quiet down even a little bit, is wanting to check the scale. I just get this intense, burning need to go home, strip down, and step on the scale to see exactly what that fried food or that church plate did to my body right then and there. 

So, no, there's no big childhood trauma. The panic is just... it's right now. It's every time I eat those things. I just don't know how else to explain it to you so you understand that it's happening right now, not ten years ago.
Do you think there's a specific part of your body that, if it were a different size, would make you feel better about your weight?

I mean... I feel like I'm taking crazy pills here, didn't I literally just say this? I know I just talked about this when you asked about my perception a few minutes ago. I don't mean to get snappy, I just... I really feel like I'm repeating myself a lot. But yes, to answer your question, there are specific parts. Like I was saying earlier, it's my stomach and my thighs. 

If those were just smaller, if they just looked right, I wouldn't have this constant, heavy weight on me all the time. It's like... when I look in the mirror before class—my GED class, I mean—or when I'm getting dressed for softball, those are the parts I'm immediately staring at. My eyes just zoom right in on them. And they still look bigger than they should. It doesn't matter what I do, they just protrude, they take up too much space, and I can see exactly how much extra is there. 

And it's not just a passing thought where I can go, "Oh, I don't like that," and move on. It completely dictates my entire mood. Like I was trying to explain before, seeing those parts look so big... it can make me feel like I’m either doing good or failing for the whole day. It's like a switch flips in my brain the second I look in that mirror. If my thighs look wide, or my stomach is sticking out even a fraction of an inch, I carry that feeling of absolute failure with me out the door. I'll be sitting in class, trying to focus on math or whatever, and all I can think about is how my stomach feels against the waistband of my jeans. Or I'll be at softball, and instead of focusing on the game, I'm just feeling my thighs rub together when I run, feeling like a total, absolute failure. 

But if they were just smaller... if they were a different size and actually looked flat and small the way they're supposed to when I check the mirror in the morning? Then I'd feel like I was doing good. I'd feel light, I'd feel in control. I wouldn't have to spend my entire shift at the warehouse obsessing over every time I bend over to tape a box. So yeah, my stomach and my thighs. If those were different, I wouldn't feel like I was constantly failing at everything.
Is there something specific that happens when you eat that makes you afraid of gaining weight?

Okay, I really, really don't mean to be rude, but are you actually listening to my answers? Or is there just a checklist of questions you have to get through? Because I swear I have answered this exact thing like three times now today. 

But, okay, fine, I will explain it again. Maybe I can go into more detail so you see what I mean, because I really need you to understand this. 

When I eat... say, if I eat something like the fried food they always leave sitting out in the break room at the warehouse, or if I'm at church and I get pressured into taking a big plate of food at the fellowship hall... the specific thing that happens is just pure panic. I get so scared that it’s going to show on me right away. And I mean *right away*. Like, I swallow a bite of whatever greasy thing was in the break room, and my brain instantly tells me my stomach is pushing out further against my jeans. I can almost physically feel it happening, like the food is just instantly turning into fat on my body the second it goes down my throat. 

And then I just can't let it go. I can't just digest it and move on with my life. I will keep thinking about it, over and over and over. I'll go back to my packing station, and for the rest of my shift, every single time I move or bend over to grab tape for a box, I'm just obsessing over what I ate and how much bigger I must look now. It drives me absolutely crazy. It just plays on a loop in my head—"You ate that, it's showing, you're bigger"—until all I want to do is check the scale. I just get this desperate, clawing need to rush home, lock myself in the bathroom, and step on the scale to see exactly how much weight I just gained from that one meal. 

So... yeah, that's what happens. I eat the fried food or the big plate at church, I panic that it's instantly showing, I obsess over it for hours, and then I have to weigh myself. That's the cycle. I really hope that makes sense this time.
Is it the calories in the food or the type of food itself that makes you afraid of gaining weight?

I... wow. Okay. I honestly feel like I'm on a hidden camera show right now or something. I literally just answered this. I just told you exactly what happens with the food. 

But, okay, calories or the type of food. It's... I guess it's the type of food. Because, like I literally just said, if I eat something like fried food from the break room, or if I'm stuck with a big plate at church, I'm not necessarily sitting there adding up the math of the calories in my head right in that exact moment. It's the actual food itself that freaks me out. It's the grease, it's the heaviness, it's knowing what that specific kind of food does to a person's body. 

And like I have been trying to explain to you over and over today, when I eat that kind of stuff, I get so unbelievably scared that it’s going to show on me right away. Instantly. It's not about a number on a nutrition label, it's about feeling like my stomach is immediately expanding over my jeans because of what I just swallowed. And because I'm so scared of that happening, I’ll just keep thinking about it. Over and over and over. I'll be back at my packing station, grabbing boxes, pulling tape, and my brain is just obsessing over that fried chicken or whatever it was, and the panic just builds and builds until all I want to do is check the scale. I get that desperate, burning urge to go home, take my clothes off, and step on the scale to see the exact damage that specific type of food just did to me. 

So, yes, it's the type of food that triggers all of that. I just... I really, really hope we can talk about something else now, because I don't think I can describe the warehouse break room to you one more time.
Is your fear of gaining weight more about the number on the scale or how your body looks to you?

Okay, I... I really don't know what to do here. I am literally just repeating myself over and over and over again. Are you actually writing any of this down? Because I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall. 

It's both! They are connected! I don't know how else to explain this to you, but I'm going to try one more time, and I really, really need you to hear me this time. It's both, because one leads directly to the other. Like I have been saying all afternoon... if I eat something like the fried food they bring into the break room at the warehouse, or if I'm at church and someone forces a big plate on me, my immediate thought—my absolute first, terrifying thought—is about how it looks. I get so incredibly scared that it's going to show on me right away. I'll just be standing there, and I can almost feel my stomach pushing out against my clothes, like the food is just instantly expanding on my body. 

So, yes, it starts with how my body looks. But because I get so panicked about how it looks, I can't let it go. I'll keep thinking about it for the entire rest of my shift. I'll be taping boxes, walking around the warehouse floor, and just obsessing over how huge I must look now, and that panic just builds and builds and builds. And *that* is what drives me to the scale. I get so desperate and overwhelmed by the thought of it showing on my body that I want to check the scale the second I get home. I have to see the number to confirm the damage. 

So the fear is about how it looks, which makes me obsess over it, which makes me need to see the number on the scale to know exactly how bad it is. They are the exact same fear. They feed into each other. Please, please tell me you understand what I'm saying this time so we can talk about something else.
Is there a particular body part that you are most concerned about when you think about gaining weight?

Well, I mean, I did just say that I constantly feel like my stomach is pushing out against my jeans, so I feel like that was a pretty big clue. But yes, if you want the exact specifics, it’s my stomach. And my thighs. Those are the two main things that just completely run my life. 

It’s like an everyday obsession. Every single morning, it’s the exact same routine. When I look in the mirror before I head out to the warehouse for my shift, or like, on the weekends before I go play softball with my rec league, I will just stand there staring at myself. I'll turn to the side, I'll pull my shirt tight, I'll stand with my feet together to check the gap between my legs, and my stomach and thighs just still look bigger than they should. No matter what I do, they just always look wrong to me. Too wide, too heavy, just... bigger than they have any right to be. 

And I can't even begin to explain how much power that reflection has over me. What I see in that mirror in those five minutes before I leave the house completely dictates my reality. It can make me feel like I’m either doing good or failing for the whole entire day. If I look in the mirror and my stomach seems even a tiny bit rounder, or my thighs look like they're touching too much, that’s it. The day is ruined. I am failing.
